definition: The 99th percentile latency: 99% of requests finish faster than this number, and 1% are slower. It exposes the tail that an average hides.
How long one request takes from the user's point of view. Usually measured in milliseconds.
How many requests or jobs a system completes per unit of time, such as requests per second.
The fraction of time a system is able to serve requests. 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime per year.
A promise about which version of the data a reader sees. Strong consistency means everyone sees the latest committed write.
A behavior the system must perform: book a slot, cancel an appointment, send a reminder.
A quality target the system must meet: latency, availability, consistency, security, cost or maintainability.
What you give up when you choose one design over another. Every meaningful design decision has one.
The part of the system that limits the whole. Speeding up anything else does not raise total throughput until the bottleneck moves.
A fast copy of data kept closer to the reader. It trades freshness and memory for lower latency and less database load.
Time to live: how long a cached value is allowed to exist before it must be refreshed or evicted.
The fraction of cache reads served from the copy: hits / (hits + misses). Database load follows the miss rate.
A caching pattern where the application checks the cache first, reads the database on a miss, and writes the copy back.
A caching pattern where the cache client fetches from the database on a miss, moving the fill logic out of application code.
A caching pattern that writes the database and the cache synchronously before returning, keeping the copy warm at the cost of a second write.
A caching pattern that acknowledges a write from the cache and flushes to the database later. Fast, but acknowledged writes can be lost if the cache fails.
Dropping or replacing cached copies when the source changes. Usually a delete after commit, backed by a TTL for missed paths.
Many concurrent requests miss the same popular key and rebuild it at once, flooding the database with identical work.
A large set of keys expires at the same moment, so the database receives the combined miss load in one burst.
Repeated lookups of keys that do not exist. Every request misses and reaches the database unless absence is cached or filtered.
A single key that receives a disproportionate share of traffic, enough to saturate one cache node or shard.
Least recently used: an eviction policy that discards the key not read for the longest time. Good for temporal locality, vulnerable to scans.
Least frequently used: an eviction policy that discards the key with the fewest reads. Protects hot keys from bursts but needs aging as popularity changes.
Caching a not-found result for a short TTL so repeated lookups of missing keys do not reach the database.
Coalescing concurrent misses for the same key so only one request rebuilds the value and the others wait for its result.
A data structure that makes a particular lookup fast, at the cost of extra storage and slower writes.
The column or columns that uniquely identify a row in a table.
A column that points to a primary key in another table, expressing a relationship between rows.
A server that sits in front of application servers and forwards requests to them. It can handle TLS, routing, compression and load balancing.
A reverse proxy that gives a pool of servers one address and chooses where each request or connection goes.
A server that keeps no user session state between requests. Any server can handle the next request, which makes horizontal scaling easier.
A fixed set of open database connections reused by a process. The total across the fleet is what the database must accept.
A copy of a database kept on another machine. Read replicas serve reads; a primary handles writes.
How far a replica is behind the primary. A read from a lagging replica can miss a write that just succeeded.
Promoting a replica or standby to take over when the primary fails.
A horizontal slice of data stored on its own database. Sharding splits data across machines, usually by a shard key.
A buffer that holds work until a worker is ready to process it. Queues absorb spikes and decouple the producer from the consumer.
An operation that produces the same result even if it runs twice. Retries are safe only when the operation is idempotent.
A unique key attached to a request so the server can detect a retry and return the original result instead of doing the work twice.
A cap on how many requests a client may make in a time window. It protects the system from bots, bugs and abuse.
The HTTP status code for a request rejected by a rate limit. A Retry-After header can tell the client when to try again.
Waiting longer between retries, often with random jitter, so a struggling service is not hammered by synchronized retries.
A failure detector that stops calling a failing service for a while and returns a fallback instead.
Deliberately rejecting some requests under overload so the rest can still succeed.
During a network partition, a distributed system can preserve consistency or availability, but not both. It is a partition-time choice, not a permanent label.
A minimum number of nodes that must agree for a read or write to count, often a majority of replicas.
A record that something happened, such as order placed or payment captured. Events let services react without direct calls.
A sequence of local transactions across services, with compensating actions that undo earlier steps if a later step fails.
A table that stores events in the same transaction as the business change, so a background publisher can send them reliably.
A content delivery network: servers close to users that cache static and sometimes dynamic content.
Storage for files such as photos and videos, addressed by a key and served over HTTP rather than stored in a database row.
Giving one machine more CPU, memory or disk. Simple, but it has a hardware ceiling and leaves a single failure domain.
Running several identical servers behind a load balancer so capacity can grow and one failure does not stop the service.
A probe that decides whether a server should receive traffic. A shallow check tests the process; a readiness check tests its dependencies.
A short-lived URL that grants permission to upload or download one object, so the client can talk to storage without the API carrying the bytes.
The source a CDN fetches from on a cache miss. Origin load follows the miss rate, not total traffic.
The ability to understand a system's internal state from its outputs: logs, metrics, traces and events.
Following one request across many services by passing a shared trace ID and recording each span.
A way to assign keys to servers so adding or removing a server moves only a small fraction of the keys.
A compact probabilistic set that can say definitely not present or maybe present. It never has false negatives, but it can have false positives.
A probabilistic counter that estimates the number of distinct items using a small, fixed amount of memory.
A probabilistic frequency counter that uses a fixed-size table and can overestimate counts, but never underestimate them.
A string encoding of a geographic area. Nearby prefixes usually mean nearby places, which makes proximity search cheaper.
A tree keyed by characters, used for autocomplete and prefix search.
A map from a term to the documents that contain it. It is the basic structure behind full-text search.
A balanced tree optimized for disk reads. It is the default index structure in many relational databases.
A log-structured merge tree: writes go to memory and sorted files, then merge in the background. It favors write throughput over read simplicity.
A durable log written before data pages change, so a database can recover after a crash.
A hash tree that lets two replicas find differing blocks without comparing every block.
A time-ordered unique ID made from a timestamp, machine ID and sequence number.
A logical counter that gives a partial order to events without relying on synchronized physical clocks.
A per-node logical clock that can detect whether two events are ordered or concurrent.
A way for nodes to spread membership and failure information by periodically telling a few peers.
A lock with an expiry time. If the holder pauses too long, the lease can expire and another node can take over.
A monotonically increasing number attached to a lease, so a stale lock holder's writes can be rejected.
A conflict-free replicated data type: a data structure that can merge concurrent updates without losing information.
Sending one event or request to many destinations. Fan-out on write builds feeds ahead of time; fan-out on read builds them when requested.
A counter split across many rows or keys, then summed, to avoid one hot row under extreme write load.
Recovery point objective: how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time.
Recovery time objective: how long the system may take to come back after a failure.
A continuously updated read-only copy of a database that serves read queries and can be promoted during failover.
The database node that accepts writes and is the source of truth for replicas.
A guarantee that after a user writes, that user’s subsequent reads see the write.
A guarantee that a user never sees data go backwards in time across successive reads.
Replication where the primary commits without waiting for a replica to acknowledge, trading a small data-loss window for normal write latency.
Replication where the primary waits for a replica to acknowledge before confirming a commit, reducing RPO at the cost of latency and availability.
The step that turns a read replica into the writable primary during failover.
A failure where two nodes both believe they are primary and accept writes, leaving divergent histories.
Restoring a base backup and replaying archived WAL to a chosen moment, used to recover from deletes or corruption.
A scheduled test that restores a backup into a clean environment, validates the data and measures recovery time.
